title: Trump’s New Coercive Toolkit
gist: On August 7 the US Senate passed an amended Russian sanctions bill letting the president levy tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas; if the House agrees, secondary tariffs become a standard sanctions instrument. Gavekal frames this as part of a broader fusion of tariffs, sanctions, industrial policy and export controls for geopolitical ends, with India the most exposed flashpoint.

themes.theme: Secondary tariffs as a sanctions instrument

insights.claim: On August 7, 2026 the US Senate passed an amended Russian sanctions bill authorizing the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the world's five largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A live legislative vehicle that could put punitive tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian energy — screen exposure to those importers and to Russian crude flows.

insights.so_what: Passage is not a done deal; the House vote is the binary event to watch before pricing in secondary tariff risk.

insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A durable regime shift: third countries trading with sanctioned states would carry a permanent tariff tail risk, not just headline risk.

insights.claim: As Trump rebuilds his tariff regime, he is increasingly making access to the US market conditional on behavior that has little to do with bilateral trade.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Tariff risk can no longer be modeled from trade balances alone — a country's foreign policy conduct is now an input to its US market access.

insights.claim: Tariffs, sanctions, industrial policy and export controls are being integrated into a single toolkit used to pursue geopolitical ends.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Policy instruments that used to be analyzed separately now move together, so a sanctions headline can carry immediate tariff and export-control consequences.

insights.claim: This fusion of coercive economic tools risks reigniting international trade disputes, most notably with India.

insights.so_what: India is flagged as the most likely flashpoint — a reason to watch Indian export-facing assets and the rupee for renewed US trade friction.
